sections.title: Electric Potential Energy: Potential Difference
objectives: Define electric potential and electric potential energy.
Describe the relationship between potential difference and electrical potential energy.
Explain electron volt and its usage in submicroscopic process.
Determine electric potential energy given potential difference and amount of charge.

misconceptions.claim: Potential is the same everywhere around a point charge.
misconceptions.correction: It falls as one over the distance, so it is only equal on a sphere around the charge.

misconceptions.claim: Potential difference between two points is the force on a unit charge placed between them.
misconceptions.correction: That is the electric field. The potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between the two points.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-3, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the field definition as an option.

summary: Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge.

The potential difference between points A and B, VB–VA, defined to be the change in potential energy of a charge q moved from A to B, is equal to the change in potential energy divided by the charge, Potential difference is commonly called voltage, represented by the symbol ΔV. Δ V = ΔPE q and ΔPE = qΔV .
An electron volt is the energy given to a fundamental charge accelerated through a potential difference of 1 V. In equation form, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10 –19 C 1 V = 1.60 × 10 –19 C 1 J/C = 1.60 × 10 –19 J.

sections.title: Electric Potential in a Uniform Electric Field
objectives: Describe the relationship between voltage and electric field.
Derive an expression for the electric potential and electric field.
Calculate electric field strength given distance and voltage.

misconceptions.claim: Electric field is measured in volts.
misconceptions.correction: Electric field is measured in volts per metre or newtons per coulomb. The volt is the unit of potential difference.
misconceptions.signal: Field and potential are different quantities.

misconceptions.claim: The electric potential is the same everywhere in a uniform electric field.
misconceptions.correction: The potential changes linearly with distance along the field, V = Ed. Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to the field.
misconceptions.signal: A uniform field has a constant gradient of potential.

summary: The voltage between points A and B is V AB = Ed E = V AB d (uniform E - field only), where d is the distance from A to B, or the distance between the plates.

In equation form, the general relationship between voltage and electric field is E=–ΔVΔs, where Δs is the distance over which the change in potential, ΔV, takes place. The minus sign tells us that E points in the direction of decreasing potential.) The electric field is said to be the gradient (as in grade or slope) of the electric potential.

authored_exercises.stem: In a uniform electric field, how are the potential difference, field strength and distance related?
authored_exercises.answer: V = Ed, where d is the distance along the field.
solution: The field is uniform, so the potential changes at a constant rate.
The change in potential is the field times the distance along it.
V = Ed.

sections.title: Electrical Potential Due to a Point Charge
objectives: Explain point charges and express the equation for electric potential of a point charge.
Distinguish between electric potential and electric field.
Determine the electric potential of a point charge given charge and distance.

misconceptions.claim: The potential of a point charge falls with the square of the distance, like the field.
misconceptions.correction: The potential falls as $1/r$. It is the electric field that falls as $1/r^2$, because the field is the gradient of the potential.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-4, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the square law as an option.

summary: Electric potential of a point charge is V=kQ/r.

Electric potential is a scalar, and electric field is a vector. Addition of voltages as numbers gives the voltage due to a combination of point charges, whereas addition of individual fields as vectors gives the total electric field.

sections.title: Equipotential Lines
objectives: Explain equipotential lines and equipotential surfaces.
Describe the action of grounding an electrical appliance.
Compare electric field and equipotential lines.

misconceptions.claim: A voltmeter measures the energy of a charge.
misconceptions.correction: It measures the potential difference between two points, and that difference times the charge is the energy.

summary: An equipotential line is a line along which the electric potential is constant.
An equipotential surface is a three-dimensional version of equipotential lines.
Equipotential lines are always perpendicular to electric field lines.

authored_exercises.answer: A line along which the electric potential is the same at every point.
solution: Potential is a scalar value at each point.
An equipotential line joins points with the same value.
It is always perpendicular to the electric field lines.

sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source section on Equipotential Lines has no worked example; the teaching text derives the key results and the practice set applies them.

sections.title: Capacitors and Dielectrics
objectives: Describe the action of a capacitor and define capacitance.
Explain parallel plate capacitors and their capacitances.
Discuss the process of increasing the capacitance of a dielectric.
Determine capacitance given charge and voltage.

misconceptions.claim: A capacitor stores charge but no energy.
misconceptions.correction: Separating charge stores energy in the electric field. The energy is ½CV², and it can be released when the capacitor discharges.
misconceptions.signal: A charged capacitor can light a lamp or fire a defibrillator.

misconceptions.claim: The capacitance of a capacitor depends on how much charge it currently holds.
misconceptions.correction: Capacitance depends on the geometry and the dielectric. For a given capacitor C is fixed; Q and V change together as Q = CV.
misconceptions.signal: C is a property of the device, not of the charge.

summary: A capacitor is a device used to store charge.
The amount of charge Q a capacitor can store depends on two major factors—the voltage applied and the capacitor’s physical characteristics, such as its size.
The capacitance C is the amount of charge stored per volt, or C=QV.

authored_exercises.answer: The charge stored per unit potential difference, C = Q/V.
solution: A capacitor stores separated charge.
The more charge it holds for a given voltage, the larger its capacitance.
C = Q/V.

sections.title: Capacitors in Series and Parallel
objectives: Derive expressions for total capacitance in series and in parallel.
Identify series and parallel parts in the combination of connection of capacitors.
Calculate the effective capacitance in series and parallel given individual capacitances.

misconceptions.claim: Capacitors in parallel carry the same charge.
misconceptions.correction: Capacitors in parallel have the same voltage across them. Their charges add, and the total capacitance is the sum.
misconceptions.signal: Parallel branches share voltage, not charge.

misconceptions.claim: Capacitors in series have the same voltage across each one.
misconceptions.correction: Capacitors in series carry the same charge. Their voltages add, and the reciprocals of their capacitances add.
misconceptions.signal: Series components share charge, not voltage.

summary: Total capacitance in series 1CS=1C1+1C2+1C3+...
Total capacitance in parallel Cp=C1+C2+C3+...
If a circuit contains a combination of capacitors in series and parallel, identify series and parallel parts, compute their capacitances, and then find the total.

authored_exercises.stem: A 6.0-µF capacitor is connected in series with a 2.0-µF capacitor, and that pair is connected in parallel with a 4.0-µF capacitor. Find the total capacitance of the combination and the total charge it stores when it is connected across a 12-V battery.
solution: The series pair: 1/C_series = 1/6.0 + 1/2.0 = 0.667 µF⁻¹, so C_series = 1.5 µF.
The parallel branch adds directly: C_total = 1.5 + 4.0 = 5.5 µF.
Q = C_total V = 5.5 × 10⁻⁶ F × 12 V = 66 µC.

sections.title: Energy Stored in Capacitors
objectives: List some uses of capacitors.
Express in equation form the energy stored in a capacitor.
Explain the function of a defibrillator.

misconceptions.claim: Doubling the charge on a capacitor doubles the energy stored.
misconceptions.correction: At fixed capacitance, E = Q²/(2C), so doubling Q quadruples the energy. If the voltage doubles, E = ½CV² also quadruples.
misconceptions.signal: Energy depends on the square of charge or voltage.

misconceptions.claim: A defibrillator stores its energy in a resistor.
misconceptions.correction: It stores energy in a large capacitor and delivers it through electrodes and the body’s resistance in a controlled pulse.
misconceptions.signal: The capacitor is the energy store; the resistor shapes the discharge.

summary: Capacitors are used in a variety of devices, including defibrillators, microelectronics such as calculators, and flash lamps, to supply energy.

The energy stored in a capacitor can be expressed in three ways: Ecap=QV2=CV22=Q22C, where Q is the charge, V is the voltage, and C is the capacitance of the capacitor. The energy is in joules when the charge is in coulombs, voltage is in volts, and capacitance is in farads.

sec-6:exr-91.stem: A 10.0-µF parallel-plate capacitor is connected across an 8.00-kV supply. (a) What charge is stored? (b) How much energy is stored? (c) The space between the plates is then filled with a dielectric of constant 2.50 while the supply stays connected. What charge is stored now?
solution: (c) At fixed voltage, $Q$ scales with $C$, so $Q'=κQ=2.50(80.0mC)=200mC$ .

sec-3:exr-41.stem: Consider three parallel conducting plates, with a space of 3.0 cm between them. The leftmost one is at a potential of +45 V, the middle one is held at ground, and the rightmost is at a potential of -75 V. The middle plate has holes so that the electron can pass through. What is the magnitude of the average electric field on an electron traveling between the plates?
solution: Between the left and middle plates: $E_{1}=45\ \mathrm{V}/0.030\ \mathrm{m}=1500\ \mathrm{V/m}$.
Between the middle and right plates: $E_{2}=75\ \mathrm{V}/0.030\ \mathrm{m}=2500\ \mathrm{V/m}$.
Over the whole 6.0 cm path the potential changes by 120 V, so the average field is $120\ \mathrm{V}/0.060\ \mathrm{m}=2000\ \mathrm{V/m}$.

sec-6:exr-64.stem: A student was changing one dimension of a square parallel-plate capacitor and measuring the charge stored in a circuit with a fixed battery voltage. The student forgot which dimension was varied and did not record the units. The measurements are: side length (arbitrary units) 1.00, 1.10, 1.20, 1.30; charge ($\mu\mathrm{C}$) 0.50, 0.61, 0.71, 0.86. Which dimension was varied?

options.text: Both the area and the length of a side

solution: For a parallel-plate capacitor, $C=\epsilon_{0}A/d$ and $Q=CV$, so the charge is proportional to the plate area if the battery voltage is fixed.
Test the area hypothesis: if the area varied directly, $Q/x$ would be constant. The values are 0.50, 0.555, 0.592, and 0.662, so it is not.

Test the side-length hypothesis: if the side length $x$ varied, $A=x^{2}$ and $Q/x^{2}$ should be constant. The values are 0.50, 0.504, 0.493, and 0.509, which are nearly constant. The varied dimension was the length of a side.

options.text: it grows proportional to length squared
it shrinks proportional to length squared
